title: The Prince
author: Jacob Allee
summary: Jacob Allee opens his Great Books study guide to Machiavelli's The Prince by asking what a person's name comes to stand for, noting that Machiavelli's has become shorthand for cold calculation in pursuit of power. He describes the book as a guide for rulers on how to acquire and hold new territory, with historical examples of alliances, mercenaries, and whether it is better to be loved or feared. He grants that it is persuasive, then sets it against Christ's call to peacemaking and love of neighbor. His answer to why Christians should read it is that it exposes how powerful and unprincipled people operate in politics, business and personal relationships, and that awareness is the first step to resisting such tactics. He urges readers to be wise as serpents and innocent as doves, to separate worldly prudence from godly prudence, and to ask what they want their own names to be associated with before God. The post serves as an introduction, with section links to follow.
points: The introduction frames Machiavelli's name as a lesson in reputation, asking readers what their own names will be associated with.
Allee argues that reading The Prince is defensible for Christians because understanding unprincipled power tactics is the first step to resisting them.
The post sets Machiavelli's assumption that moral scruple is a weakness against biblical examples such as David, Jericho and Gideon, where obeying God is the truest form of prudence.
Discernment is treated as a skill: a reader should be able to glean what is true from a worldly thinker while discarding the dross.
As the opening of a study-guide series, it shows the course's method of reading primary texts critically within a Christian framework.
quotes: The last name of Nicolo Machiavelli (1469-1527 A.D.) has come to be associated with being cold and calculated and with doing whatever it takes to come out on top.
The Prince is a guidebook, of sorts, for heads of state about how to acquire and maintain dominance over new regions.

Christians should read Machiavelli because he provides us with a useful blueprint as to how powerful, godless, and unprincipled men tend to play chess not only in politics, but also in the world of business and even in interpersonal relationships. Being aware of such tactics is the first step to combatting them.
Part of becoming a prudent and godly leader, however, is being able to understand how worldly people think without falling in line with their way of thinking.

He did not mean to use that truth for good, of course, rather, he meant it for his own self-serving purposes, to use it as a weapon for self advancement and domination, but he didn’t out and out lie about everything. The best liars lie with the truth still dripping from their mouths.
But, in fact, all of these actions were prudent in the truest sense of the word because it is always prudent to obey God and it is never prudent to do what is wicked.
Let us glean what truth we can from Machiavelli once all of the dross is taken away from the refining fire of Scripture.
